IARC concluded that there is enough evidence to link the consumption of processed meat with bowel cancer. They also stated that the risk of developing colorectal cancer is increased for those who consume processed meat. Their findings are based on the results of more than 800 studies that looked into the link between cancer and the consumption of red and processed meat.
To be more specific, processed meats are those that have been transformed to improve flavor or to preserve them. This means meats that have been smoked, cured, salted, or chemically preserved. Red meat is defined as all types of mammal muscle meat, such as beef, lamb, and pork, as well as processed meats.
In a press release, Dr. Kurt Straif, the head of the IARC working group, stated that there is sufficient evidence that processed meat causes cancer, specifically in the colon and rectum. They also said that there was enough evidence to link the consumption of red meat to colorectal cancer, as well as to pancreatic and prostate cancers, but the evidence was not as strong. The IARC classified red meat as probably carcinogenic and the consumption of processed meat as carcinogenic to humans.
The IARC also stated that it is impossible to determine the exact risk of cancer that a person takes on when they consume red and processed meat. They also admitted that more study is needed to determine the exact dose-response relationship between red and processed meat and cancer risk. According to the report, people should reduce their consumption of meat, but it is not necessary that they cut it out completely. The IARC also warned that the consumption of red and processed meat is also linked to an overall increased risk of death, and to cardiovascular disease.
The report comes at a time when more and more people are concerned about the food they eat, especially when it comes to health. With the rise of the paleo diet, and the increasing popularity of meat-free meals, the report might have an impact on people and their eating habits.

It is the fact that the cost of funding for long-term liabilities, such as pension obligations, is often negative in real terms. In other words, these long-term liabilities are being funded at negative interest rates.
In Japan, for instance, pension funds and insurance companies are currently earning negative real interest rates on 10-year Japanese government bonds, while in the eurozone the real yield on 10-year bonds is minus 0.32%. In the U.S., the real yield on 10-year Treasuries is only 0.5% and in the U.K. real yields on 10-year gilts are -0.3%. Pension funds and insurance companies, as well as other institutional investors, are, therefore, being forced to look beyond developed markets for yield, often to EMs, where yields are significantly higher. In the case of EM sovereign bonds, for instance, the real yield on 10-year bonds in Brazil, India, Indonesia, and South Korea, is in excess of 2%.
This trend has been in place for some time, but it is accelerating as developed world central banks continue to push interest rates further into negative territory and as global monetary stimulus programs continue. In Europe, for example, the European Central Bank (ECB) has a target of -0.4% on the main refinancing rate and the deposit facility, and the ECB is in the process of increasing the scale of its quantitative easing (QE) program. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) has a target of -0.1% on the overnight call rate, and it is also increasing the scale of its QE program. Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve (Fed) is likely to continue its monetary easing and the U.S. yield curve is flattening as the Fed raises interest rates and short-term rates are being driven up to levels that are increasingly at odds with negative real yields on long-term debt. Fergus is one of a small group of gardeners who have been growing Diascia personata for the past 10 years. He says it is very easy to grow and is not fussy about soil. In my garden the plant thrives in a well-drained, clay-loam in full sun and I have had no problems with pests or disease. It flowers for a good 8-10 weeks in early summer, but also produces a second flush in late summer and autumn, so it should be pruned back hard to the ground after flowering to encourage a second flush. It is also happy in containers.
The only problem with Diascia personata is that it is not available in the UK. Fergus says he grows it from cuttings, which he sends to the RHS Plant Science Department in Cambridge for propagation. It is also available from the RHS Plant Clinic in RHS Wisley and from a few specialist nurseries in Europe. I am told that the plant is also in cultivation in South Africa, so there is a possibility that it will be available here one day.
Diascia personata was discovered by the American botanist Thomas L. Pakenham in the Cape Province of South Africa in 1936 and named for its resemblance to the African daisy. It belongs to the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), and is closely related to the snapdragon. It is native to the Western Cape of South Africa, where it grows in the fynbos, a Mediterranean climate zone. Its habitat consists of steep, rocky outcrops in winter-rainfall areas, where it occurs in soil that is very rich in iron and magnesium. It is not fussy about soil pH and is tolerant of full sun and drought. It has become naturalised in some parts of Australia and in the Cape Verde Islands, where it is known as Cape daisy and is sometimes eaten as a vegetable.
